# Quantum Field Theory in Finite Volume as a Systematic Physical Framework

# Volume II — Two-Body Scattering and the Generalized Lüscher Framework

## Part V — Beyond Standard Lüscher

---

# 20. Nonlocal Interactions

## 20.1 Motivation

The conventional Lüscher framework assumes that interactions are local or effectively short-ranged compared with the spatial volume.

Specifically,

[
R \ll L,
]

where

[
R
]

denotes the interaction range.

Many physical systems violate this assumption.

Examples include:

* Effective interactions generated by integrating out heavy fields,
* Nonlocal effective field theories,
* Retarded interactions,
* Composite-particle exchange processes,
* Emergent interactions in condensed matter systems.

Finite-volume quantum field theory must therefore be generalized to accommodate nonlocal dynamics.

---

## 20.2 Nonlocal Kernels

Consider an interaction action

[
S_{\rm int}
===========

\frac12
\int d^4x, d^4y;
\phi(x),
K(x,y),
\phi(y).
]

The kernel

[
K(x,y)
]

contains spatially extended correlations.

Local interactions correspond to

[
K(x,y)
\propto
\delta(x-y).
]

---

## 20.3 Finite-Volume Bethe–Salpeter Equation

The Bethe–Salpeter kernel becomes

[
\mathcal K_L(p,p')
==================

\mathcal K_\infty(p,p')
+
\Delta\mathcal K_L(p,p').
]

Unlike local theories,

[
\Delta\mathcal K_L
]

cannot be neglected exponentially.

---

## 20.4 Modified Quantization Condition

The determinant equation becomes

[
\det
\Big[
\mathcal K^{-1}
+
F_L
+
N_L
\Big]
=====

0.

]

The operator

[
N_L
]

contains genuine nonlocal finite-volume effects.

---

## 20.5 Spectral Distortion

For local interactions,

[
\Delta E_n
\sim
e^{-mL}.
]

For nonlocal theories,

[
\Delta E_n
]

may exhibit power-law behavior:

[
\Delta E_n
\sim
L^{-\alpha}.
]

The spectral geometry is fundamentally altered.

---

## 20.6 Effective Nonlocal Range

Define

[
R_{\rm eff}
===========

\frac{
\int d^3r, r,|K(r)|
}{
\int d^3r, |K(r)|
}.
]

The standard Lüscher regime requires

[
R_{\rm eff}\ll L.
]

Outside this regime new quantization conditions emerge.

---

## 20.7 Nonlocal Reconstruction Theorem

The finite-volume spectrum determines both the scattering amplitude and the nonlocal interaction kernel provided spectral data are available over a sufficiently large family of compactifications.

---

# 21. Long-Range Forces

## 21.1 Failure of Exponential Localization

Lüscher theory relies on the exponential suppression

[
e^{-mL}.
]

Long-range forces invalidate this assumption.

Examples include:

* Coulomb interactions,
* Massless scalar exchange,
* Gravitational interactions,
* Dipole forces.

---

## 21.2 Infinite Interaction Range

For a massless mediator,

[
V(r)
\propto
\frac1r.
]

No finite interaction length exists.

The conventional derivation of finite-volume quantization conditions breaks down.

---

## 21.3 Finite-Volume Coulomb Sums

The finite-volume potential becomes

[
V_L(r)
======

\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^3}
\frac1{|r+nL|}.
]

This infinite image sum converges conditionally.

---

## 21.4 Ewald Representation

Introduce

[
V_L
===

V_{\rm short}
+
V_{\rm long}.
]

The Ewald decomposition separates rapidly and slowly convergent contributions.

This provides a mathematically well-defined finite-volume Coulomb interaction.

---

## 21.5 Modified Phase Shifts

The standard asymptotic form

[
\psi(r)
\sim
\sin(kr+\delta)
]

is replaced by Coulomb wavefunctions

[
F_\ell(\eta,kr),
\qquad
G_\ell(\eta,kr).
]

Consequently the ordinary phase shift loses direct physical meaning.

---

## 21.6 Coulomb Quantization Condition

The finite-volume determinant becomes

[
\det
\Big[
\mathcal M_C^{-1}
+
F_C
\Big]
=====

0.

]

Both quantities differ fundamentally from their short-range counterparts.

---

## 21.7 Long-Range Universality Principle

The finite-volume spectrum of any theory with massless exchange is governed by a modified geometry-dependent infrared operator replacing the ordinary Lüscher function.

---

# 22. Electromagnetic Corrections

## 22.1 Motivation

Precision lattice calculations require inclusion of quantum electrodynamics.

The fine-structure constant

[
\alpha
======

\frac{e^2}{4\pi}
]

generates measurable finite-volume effects.

---

## 22.2 Infrared Problem

Photons are massless.

Consequently

[
L\rightarrow\infty
]

and

[
k\rightarrow0
]

limits fail to commute.

A special treatment is required.

---

## 22.3 QED(_L)

The most common finite-volume prescription removes the photon zero mode:

[
A_\mu(k=0)=0.
]

This defines the finite-volume theory known as

[
\mathrm{QED}_L.
]

---

## 22.4 Universal Mass Shift

For a charged particle,

[
M(L)
====

M_\infty
+
\frac{\alpha Q^2 c_1}{L}
+
\mathcal O(L^{-2}).
]

The coefficient

[
c_1
]

depends only on geometry.

---

## 22.5 Charged Two-Body Systems

The quantization condition becomes

[
\det
\Big[
\mathcal M_{\rm QCD+QED}^{-1}
+
F_L^{\rm QED}
\Big]
=====

0.

]

Both strong and electromagnetic interactions contribute simultaneously.

---

## 22.6 Bound States with Electromagnetism

For charged bound states,

[
E_B(L)
======

E_B
+
\frac{\alpha}{L}
+
\mathcal O(L^{-2}).
]

Power-law corrections dominate over exponential terms.

---

## 22.7 Electromagnetic Reconstruction Theorem

Finite-volume spectra measured across multiple volumes uniquely determine both strong-interaction scattering parameters and electromagnetic finite-volume corrections.

---

# 23. Non-Cubic Geometries

## 23.1 Beyond the Cube

The majority of finite-volume analyses employ

[
L\times L\times L.
]

However finite-volume QFT admits arbitrary compact spatial geometries.

Examples include:

[
L_x\times L_y\times L_z,
]

rectangular tori,

prisms,

and generalized compact manifolds.

---

## 23.2 Anisotropic Momentum Quantization

For a rectangular volume,

[
p_i
===

\frac{2\pi n_i}{L_i}.
]

Momentum spacing becomes direction dependent.

---

## 23.3 Geometry Tensor

Define

[
G_{ij}
======

\mathrm{diag}
(L_x^{-2},
L_y^{-2},
L_z^{-2}).
]

The free spectrum becomes

[
E^2
===

m^2
+
(2\pi)^2
G_{ij}n^in^j.
]

---

## 23.4 Generalized Zeta Functions

The cubic zeta function is replaced by

[
Z_{lm}^{(G)}(s;q^2).
]

Its structure depends explicitly on the geometry tensor.

---

## 23.5 Symmetry Reduction

The cubic group

[
O_h
]

is replaced by smaller symmetry groups.

Partial-wave mixing increases.

New irreducible representations emerge.

---

## 23.6 Geometric Optimization

Different geometries probe different momentum shells.

Consequently geometric variation provides additional information for amplitude reconstruction.

---

## 23.7 Geometry Reconstruction Principle

Finite-volume spectra measured across multiple compact geometries contain substantially more dynamical information than spectra obtained from cubic volumes alone.

---

# 24. Curved Compact Spaces

## 24.1 Motivation

Nothing in quantum field theory requires the compact space to be flat.

The most general finite-volume formulation should permit compact curved manifolds

[
(\Sigma,g).
]

---

## 24.2 Curved-Space Laplacian

The Laplace operator becomes

[
\Delta_g
========

\frac1{\sqrt g}
\partial_i
\left(
\sqrt g,
g^{ij}
\partial_j
\right).
]

Momentum eigenstates are replaced by geometric eigenmodes

[
u_n(x).
]

---

## 24.3 Spectral Geometry

The eigenvalue equation is

[
-\Delta_g u_n
=============

\lambda_n u_n.
]

Finite-volume spectra now depend simultaneously on:

[
g_{ij},
\qquad
\mathcal M,
\qquad
L.
]

---

## 24.4 Curvature Corrections

The heat-kernel expansion yields

[
K(s)
====

(4\pi s)^{-3/2}
\Big[
a_0
+
a_1 s
+
a_2 s^2
+\cdots
\Big].
]

Curvature enters through

[
a_1
===

\frac16
\int_\Sigma R,dV.
]

---

## 24.5 Curved-Space Quantization Condition

The determinant equation generalizes to

[
\det
\Big[
\mathcal M^{-1}
+
F_g
\Big]
=====

0.

]

The geometric operator

[
F_g
]

depends upon the complete spectral geometry of the manifold.

---

## 24.6 Curved-Space Scattering

Scattering is no longer described relative to plane waves.

Instead it is formulated through transitions between eigenmodes of

[
\Delta_g.
]

The finite-volume spectrum becomes a geometric scattering observable.

---

## 24.7 Spectral Geometry Conjecture

The complete scattering dynamics of a quantum field theory on a compact manifold are encoded in the joint spectrum of

[
(H,\Delta_g).
]

This extends the inverse spectral program developed in Volume I.

---

## 24.8 Generalized Compactification Theorem

Lüscher theory is the special case of a flat cubic torus:

[
(T^3,\delta_{ij}).
]

The fundamental finite-volume framework is instead the quantization of quantum fields on arbitrary compact spectral manifolds.

---

# Conclusions of Part V

The standard Lüscher framework occupies only a restricted region within the full landscape of finite-volume quantum field theory. Its assumptions—local interactions, short-range forces, negligible electromagnetic effects, flat cubic geometry, and translational invariance—are sufficient for many practical applications but are not fundamental requirements of the underlying theory.

By extending the formalism to nonlocal interactions, long-range forces, electromagnetic fields, anisotropic compactifications, and curved compact manifolds, finite-volume QFT becomes a genuinely geometric framework. The central object is no longer a particular zeta function associated with a cubic box but a universal geometric operator encoding the spectral properties of compact space itself.

The principal conclusion of Part V is that finite-volume scattering theory is naturally a theory of quantum fields on compact spectral manifolds. Standard Lüscher quantization emerges as the simplest member of a much broader class of geometric quantization conditions. This perspective prepares the transition from two-body scattering theory to the genuinely new many-body finite-volume dynamics that form the subject of Volume III.
